A ready reference for doctoral researchers

Beyond the PromptEthics and human judgement in AI-assisted research

What publishers and journals ask of you when you use generative AI, stage by stage, from the first idea to peer review. Use it as a map, and check your target journal before you submit.

Walk the research journey Do I need to disclose? Start a use log

Disclaimer This website was created using AI, and AI can make mistakes. Verify anything you rely on against the original sources and your target journal's current policy.

01 · Common ground

Publishers word their policies differently, but the same four commitments appear in all of them.

Choose a commitment to see what it asks of you. Scholars still ask the questions, own the choices and stand behind the claims (Gopal et al., 2025).

02 · The research journey

Eight stages, the same three questions at each: what the tool helps with, what goes wrong, and what stays human.

Select a stage. Each one links to the evidence behind it and the practical habits the journals recommend. Use the arrows at the bottom to move through the journey in order.

03 · Levels of use

The level of use matters more than the tool. Framing, interpretation and contribution remain human.

Gopal et al. (2025) describe three roles a system can play. Journals draw the line at the third, because the link between the author and the claim is broken.

Encouraged

Copy editor

Improves expression: clarity, tone, consistent terminology. The ideas, claims and structure remain yours, and every change can be reviewed line by line.

Encouraged with controls

Research assistant

Retrieves, scaffolds code and stress-tests designs. You decide what to accept, and you keep the record of what it did.

Discouraged

Super-collaborator

Proposes the framing and the theory while the human only approves. If your work drifts here, step back to the research-assistant level.

Four decisions that stay yours

QuestionYou decide what is worth asking.
HypothesisYou state what you expect and why.
Construct definitionYou decide exactly what each concept means.
Identification choiceYou decide how the design shows cause.
A model can enumerate reasons; it cannot be the reason we believe a claim.Gopal et al. (2025), Information Systems Research

04 · How things fail

Fluency is cheap now, so credibility has to come from the process.

Several journals tested these tools directly. Open each failure mode to see what they found.

Fabricated sources

Asked for important papers on a topic, ChatGPT mixed fabricated references in with real ones. Asked to summarise a recently published ISR paper, it invented a title, a set of authors and a set of claims.

Susarla et al. (2023)

Fluent but wrong

Asked to critique a published qualitative study, the tool wrote like a novice reviewer. It missed theoretical sampling, framed the study around measurement and scales, and described methods the study did not use. It sounded confident and misread the work.

Susarla et al. (2023)

Spurious findings

An AI system that mined regulations and wrote up whatever was significant produced professional-looking papers. Pointed at non-US securities regulations, which should matter little to US firms, it still produced many papers with spurious results and unsubstantiated arguments.

Ciconte et al. (2026)

Sameness

AI ideas tend toward small, incremental improvements, and ideas across groups become less diverse. Because the models reflect what they were trained on, they tend to hand back what is already common.

De Freitas et al. (2025); Susarla et al. (2023)

05 · Toolkit

Practical tools for the moments that matter: disclosing, keeping a record, submitting and reviewing.

Your checklist ticks are kept in this browser only, so you can come back to them. Nothing you select here is sent anywhere.

Do I need to disclose this use?

Choose what the tool did. The answer reflects the common ground across publishers and journals. Journals differ, so the safe habit is to check, and when in doubt, disclose.

Sources: Gatrell et al. (2024); Roberson (2026); Gopal et al. (2025); Huang et al. (2026)

The use log

A use log is the practical form of provenance. A spreadsheet or a plain text file is enough. Start it on the first day, not when a reviewer asks.

FieldWhy it mattersExample entry
Tool and versionTools change underneath you.Claude Opus 5.5, via claude.ai
Date and settingsThe same prompt can give a different answer.23 Oct 2026; default settings; no files uploaded
Prompt and contextShows what was actually asked."List rival explanations for the effect in Table 3"
Output kept or rejectedShows where your decision entered.Kept two of five; rejected three as untestable
Verification stepWhat was checked, and by whom.Checked each against the cited papers myself

Submission checklist

Run through these five checks before you submit. Policies change between submissions, so the last item matters every time.

0 of 5

Sources: Gatrell et al. (2024); Roberson (2026); Gopal et al. (2025); Blanchard et al. (2025)

When you review work that used AI

Four questions from the Information Systems Research editorials. Outcome-only claims that amount to "the model says so" are not evidence.

Sources: Susarla et al. (2023); Gopal et al. (2025)

  1. Is the process shown?Tools, prompts, versions and where human judgement entered.
  2. Does it pass face validity?Is it consistent with what you know of the field?
  3. Can it be falsified?Could logic or evidence show the output to be wrong?
  4. Does it need a human-run check?Ask for replication when the stakes are high.

06 · The wider questions

Beyond compliance: what research should still look like when machines can draft, search and critique.

Gaps in current policiesWhere the rules cannot yet reach.
Detection
Misuse is hard to spot with certainty, by software or by people.
Enforcement
Many safeguards depend on the author's word, which is why editors ask for verifiable records such as prompts, logs and code.
Materiality
When does assistance become worth declaring? Provide records where AI materially contributed to analysis or evidence.
Good faith
Policies assume honesty. Some editors argue that is not enough and call for training, review protocols and audits.

Grimes et al. (2023); Gatrell et al. (2024); Gopal et al. (2025)

BiasWhat the model has read shapes what it returns.
Opaque training data
We rarely know what the model has read, so we cannot judge how far its answers apply.
Dominant methods set the standard
Mainstream venues and English-language work are over-weighted. A naive search on gig-platform governance, for example, can favour fairness metrics and sideline labour studies and Global South scholarship.
Pluralism narrows
Minority views drop out of view. Search beyond top venues and beyond English, and rotate the lenses you ask the tool to apply.

Susarla et al. (2023); Gopal et al. (2025)

AI and theorisingThree scenarios to think with, not findings.
Specialisation
AI across empirical work; theorising protected as human territory.
Substitution
Data-driven theorising led by AI crowds out paradigm-based theorising.
Transformation
Theorising becomes an AI-enhanced workflow, sliced into semi-autonomous steps.

Risks to watch: a "theory vending machine" that generates constructs without scrutiny, meta-conformity when everyone asks the same tools, and vocabulary borrowed from AI output. Manning's article is a viewpoint, so these are arguments, not evidence.

Manning (2026); Roberson (2026)

Your doctoral trainingBuild the underlying skill first.
New competencies
Prompt and context design, output validation, bias detection, and deciding what to delegate.
Risks to guard against
Skill atrophy, skipped learning, metrics over meaning, and a system flooded with manuscripts.

You need enough independent knowledge to judge what a tool returns, not only to prompt it.

Gopal et al. (2025); Ciconte et al. (2026); Grimes et al. (2023); Susarla et al. (2023); Kosmyna et al. (2025)

EquityMake the field fairer, not only faster.
Open models
Free, shareable tools built for the discipline, so nobody depends only on expensive products.
Affordable teaching
Methods that work with the tools your institution can actually provide.
Shared prompts and data
Share the working materials, not just the final paper. Your use log can help others too.

Gopal et al. (2025)

Peer review pilotsHow conferences are testing AI in review.
Feedback to reviewers (ICLR 2025)
A tool suggested how to make reviews clearer. The reviewer decided what to accept.
An additional AI review (AAAI 2026)
One machine-written review beside the human ones, with no scores. Concerns about hallucinated claims and formulaic phrasing persisted.
Pre-submission checks (STOC 2026)
Optional, private feedback on technical rigour before formal review, not shared with the committee.

As summarised in Gopal et al. (2025)

07 · Five principles for practice

If you take five habits away, let them be these.

  1. 01Own every claim

    Accountability cannot be delegated. A tool cannot be listed as an author.

  2. 02Disclose what you used

    Plainly and specifically: tool, purpose and oversight.

  3. 03Keep the record

    So that your process can be audited by someone else.

  4. 04Verify before you trust

    Especially references, quotations, numbers and code.

  5. 05Protect what is entrusted to you

    A participant's words, or an author's unpublished manuscript.

The tool proposes, the human scholar disposes, and the record shows the difference.Gopal et al. (2025), Information Systems Research
